newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Serbia opposition leader nominated for Nobel prize.
newsitem.headline: Serbia opposition leader nominated for Nobel prize.

text.p: Vesna Pesic, a leader of Serbia's opposition coalition, the mayor of the Bosnian city of Tuzla and a peace activist from Croatia have been nominated for the 1997 Nobel Peace Prize by the International Peace Bureau (IPB).

Colin Arsher, secretary-general of the Geneva-based IPB, a coalition of 160 independent peace groups, said on Tuesday the three symbolised efforts to create a civil society in former Yugoslavia and were nominated for opposing war and nationalism.

"The Yugoslav wars have left an appalling trail of havoc, death and suffering. We hope the Nobel Committee will recognise a few of the people who, through this terrible chapter in European history, have resisted the dominant ideology," he said.

Pesic, one of the three heads of the Zajedno (Together) coalition, has led Belgrade's mass protests against fraud that robbed the opposition of victory in 14 Serbian cities including Belgrade at local elections on November 17.

Selim Beslagic, head of the Union of Bosnian Social Democrats and the mayor of Tuzla throughout the war in former Yugoslavia, was nominated because he is a symbol of multiethnic and multi-cultural coexistence, Archer said.

Beslagic was awarded the 1996 Sean MacBride Peace Prize -- named after the late Irish statesman who led the IPB from 1974 to 1985 and won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1974 -- for helping to preserve Tuzla's multi-ethnic composition despite the war.
The third nominee is Vesna Terselic, an activist for peace, environment and women's issues in Croatia's capital Zagreb.
"We felt these three represented a very impressive joint power of testimony for the Nobel Peace Prize," Archer said.

The IPB had nominated Nobel prize laureate Joseph Rotblat who won the $1 million award in 1995 with his anti-war Pugwash group. Originally Polish but a British citizen since 1946, Rotblat is the last survivor of the scientists who signed the Bertrand Russell-Albert Einstein manifesto against the H-bomb in the mid-1950s.
